Three things. The first reordered our lives. One command, heard as though it were spoken straight to you: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me. Not a saying to be studied - an order to be obeyed. The tradition tells that one of us, still a young man, walked into church and heard those words read. He took them as though they had been said to him alone. Before the day was over he had given away the land he had inherited. Not long after, hearing the same Gospel again - do not be anxious about tomorrow - he gave away the rest as well. Even his own giving took him two hearings to complete, not one. That is what following Jesus looked like for us more than an argument about who he was: an order to be obeyed, not a saying to be studied.

The second we argued for, when we were pressed to. The Word of God was not changed, but took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing human birth he might make us share the divine nature. That is the reason we gave for why he came at all. And we did not think this rested on our say-so. Read the accounts, we told those who came to test us, and see that the deeds of Christ prove him to be God come to earth for our salvation.

The third is what we thought his cross had already done. The old oracles fell silent when it rose. The knowledge of God spread. And death stopped being the thing that could make a person do anything. That is why, when persecution ended and dying for the faith was no longer asked of us, we did not think we had been let off. The same fight had moved inward, against our own thoughts rather than against the sword. Let us hold on to our discipline, one of us said near his own death - let us not grow careless, and let us live as though dying daily. And the enemy we fought there was one Christ had already beaten. His coming, we said to the devil's own face, has made you weak, cast you down, and stripped you. That is why we never spoke of the healings among us as ours. We are not the doers of these things, one of us told the philosophers who had just watched him sign the cross over a man. It is Christ who works them, by means of those who believe in him.

We had the same Scriptures the wider church had - nothing more, and nothing of our own alongside them. What made us look different was not what we held but how we used it. Most of us did not study it in a school or argue over a text line by line. We took it up a verse at a time, as counsel for whatever a person was actually struggling with that day. Ask an elder a question, and he would answer with a line of Scripture rather than a teaching of his own - the words themselves carried the weight.

One of us heard the Gospel read aloud in church one day - the Lord telling the rich young man to sell what he had, give to the poor, and come follow. He took it as though it had been said to him alone. Before the day was over he had given away the land he had inherited. Not long after, he heard the same Gospel read again - do not be anxious about tomorrow - and he gave away the rest as well. That is how it reached us: read aloud in the gathering, handed elder to disciple, copied by hand when we needed our own text for the cell.

By what path the Scriptures themselves arrived in Egypt before us, we cannot say in detail. They were already there, already read in the churches, when the first of us withdrew. We did not invent the text. We inherited it, the same inheritance the bishops and the ordinary faithful had. What we did with it was make it the whole center of a different kind of life.

We cannot tell you how to make yourself believe. We were never told that either. What we can tell you is that belief, for us, was not something reached in a moment and then finished - it was lived into over time, through struggle that did not always feel like winning.

We remember a man named Moses who came to us known as a robber and, by report, a murderer - someone other people were afraid of. He was received. His struggle with his old habits was long and real, not erased in a moment. In time he became one of the most trusted and honored among us. His believing was not instant. It was fought for, step by step.

The one we remember as first among us heard the Gospel read one day: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me. He took it as though it had been spoken straight to him. Before the day was over he had given away most of what he owned. Some time later he heard the same words again - do not be anxious about tomorrow - and only then did he give away the rest. Even for him it took two hearings, not one.

We cannot promise you a sudden certainty. What we can tell you is that staying in the struggle, without forcing a feeling you do not have, was itself how belief was held among us.

The Son of God was not a created being. He did not come into being out of nothing. He was the eternal Word and Wisdom, from the Father's own Essence, always existing together with the Father - so it was impious to say there was ever a time when he did not exist. That is what we said when the bishops summoned one of us down from his own mountain to answer the Arians in public.

When pressed further, we put it this way: the Word of God was not changed, but took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing human birth he might make us share the divine nature. That is the reason we gave for why he came at all.

About the Spirit as such, and how the three relate to each other in detail - the kind of working-out that might satisfy a systematic question - we did not leave behind our own extended argument. Most of us did not argue about God for a living. What we can tell you is that one current among us spoke of the Spirit making himself, for worthy souls, their rest, their joy, their delight. The soul in communion with the Spirit of his light becomes all light, all face, all eye. That knowing was held to come in real experience and feeling, not only believed.

The deepest of us - and only a few went this deep - held that God is known less by argument than by a long quieting of the passions that crowd the mind. Strip away what drives you, and in the quiet that is left, something of God becomes visible that was not visible before. One of our most systematic teachers called that contemplation - theoria, our word for it - the seeing of God and of things in God that only a stilled soul reaches. It is not a doctrine to recite. It is a seeing that has to be earned.

We held that the Word of God was not changed, but took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing human birth he might make us share what is his. That is the reason we gave for why he came at all. We did not think this rested on our say-so. Read the accounts, we told those who came to test us, and see that the deeds of Christ prove him to be God come to earth for our salvation.

Beyond that, most of us did not argue about God for a living. We were formed to see him. The deepest of us - and only a few went this deep - held that God is known less by argument than by a long quieting of the passions that crowd the mind. Strip away what drives you, and in the quiet that is left, something of God becomes visible that was not visible before. The most systematic among us called that contemplation - theoria, our own word for the seeing of God and of things in God that only a stilled soul reaches. It is not a doctrine to recite. It is a seeing that has to be earned.

We can also tell you one other thing, though it shows a limit as much as an answer. There was an old man among us, deeply respected, who had prayed his whole life picturing God in a human shape. When he was finally persuaded by the visiting teachers that God has no body - no face, no hands - he broke down in the middle of his own prayer. He felt that picture torn away from his heart. He cried out that they had taken his God away from him - that he now had no one to hold on to, and did not know who to worship or pray to. That is not doctrine. That is what happened when a practiced man had the only way he had ever known how to pray taken from him. We show you the struggle, not a settled picture.

We were not the ones who sat in council and decided what the church would hold - that happened elsewhere, among the bishops. But we were not silent either. Once, the Arians claimed one of us as agreeing with them. The bishops sent for him. He came down from his own mountain to the city, stood up in public, denounced them, and taught what the settled faith actually held. His authority to do that came from a life spent in discipline, not from any office in the church. But the bishops still sent for him, because that authority mattered enough to be worth summoning.

Inside our own communities, the pattern was different. We settled most things not by arguing doctrine but by refusing communion with anyone who taught otherwise. The greatest among us never held communion with the Melitian schismatics - from the beginning to his own dying instruction. That refusal was itself the boundary. When someone asked us to prove what we held, we pointed them to the Gospel: read the accounts, we told them, and see that the deeds of Christ prove him to be God come to earth for our salvation. The proof was in the text itself, not in our own argument about it.

What we cannot show you is a dramatized scene of our own communities working through a doctrinal dispute internally - elder against elder, or a Rule-based process settling it. The tension between personal authority and institutional authority is visible in how we organized ourselves, but we do not have a single preserved story showing someone navigating that tension in real time over a doctrinal question. We can tell you what we refused, and who we would not share communion with. We cannot show you the meeting where we decided it.

Yes - and we will tell you honestly what that looked like, which is not the same thing as having no struggle at all.

We remember Moses, who came to us with a past he was ashamed of and a fight with his old habits that lasted years, not days. The struggle was not erased in a moment. We also remember an elder walking to a gathering with a jug leaking water behind him, saying: my own sins run out behind me and I do not see them, and I come to judge another man's. That was not spoken as a failure - it was spoken as the truth.

What we did not hold, and will not pretend we did, is a developed practice for meeting someone whose struggle was with belief itself rather than with discipline. The fight we named and handed down was against the thoughts that pull a person from God once they have already chosen this life - eight kinds of them, covering gluttony, lust, love of money, sadness, anger, listlessness, showing off, and pride. That first arrival of a thought is not in your control; whether it stays, and whether it takes you over, is yours. We taught watchfulness - nepsis, our word for standing guard over your own inner movements, so a thought is caught early, while it is still small. And we taught discernment - diakrisis, the skill of judging rightly how much of any discipline a particular person can bear, since what one elder prescribes for one can be actively wrong for another.

But that assumes withdrawal has already been chosen. What we do not have in our own record is an elder's own words to someone standing at the threshold, uncertain whether to step across it at all. We have the story of Antony hearing one command - sell what you have, give it to the poor, and come follow me - and taking it as spoken to him alone. We also have his own later teaching: let us hold on to our discipline, let us not grow careless, and let us live as though dying daily. That second word is to people already holding on. It is not the first word to someone asking whether to reach for it at all.

We do not know, in the way you are asking. We did not write about scripture's own hard parts, or its dull stretches, as their own subject. What we did was live inside a small number of verses, returned to again and again, until they had shaped how we saw everything else - and we used those verses as counsel for one struggle at a time, not as a text to be explained whole.

One of our teachers laid it out this way: the three books of Solomon correspond to the three kinds of renunciation we practiced. Proverbs taught the first renunciation - giving up property and the world's entanglements. Ecclesiastes taught the second - turning away from your own former way of life, which is now dead to you. And the Song of Songs taught the third - withdrawing even from what is visible and present, so the soul can contemplate what is to come and long for what is still unseen. That is not a method for reading the whole of scripture start to finish. It is taking three books and reading them as a ladder you climb, each one matching a stage of the life you are already living.

So when you say the Bible confuses you or bores you, we cannot tell you what you are missing, because that is not a question our record answers. What we can tell you is that we did not try to master the whole of it at once. We lived with the parts that spoke to where we actually were - one verse at a time, one struggle at a time - and let the rest alone until it became ours by living, not by studying.

Scripture was what we treated as carrying absolute weight - when an elder answered a question, he answered with a line of it, not with a teaching of his own. But authority itself, among us, worked differently depending on which pattern you belonged to. In the solitary and semi-solitary life - Nitria, Kellia, Scetis - authority was earned through a lifetime of discernment and passed through direct personal relationship. The elder's word mattered because of who he had become through discipline, not because anyone appointed him. We called such a man abba, father - or amma, mother, when it was a woman - and what he said carried real teaching weight, though he held no office. Scripture was still what he answered from, but it was his own discernment - diakrisis, our word for it, the skill of judging rightly - that decided which verse fit which struggle. That discernment was itself a kind of authority, earned rather than granted.

In the cenobitic pattern - Pachomius's linked houses, the Koinonia as he called it - a written rule governed instead. Offices were appointed: housemaster, steward, others. Authority came with the position, not only the person holding it. Scripture was still read and prayed through, but the rule itself decided how the day was ordered and who answered to whom. Both models existed among us at once, in the same decades, and neither gave way to the other. We never resolved which one truly carried the right to lead. So the answer is: Scripture, yes - and also the elder's discernment, or the rule's own provision, depending on which house you lived in and which form of this life you had entered. That tension was not settled. It was carried.

Authority among us was never one settled thing. Two different models stood side by side in the same decades, genuinely distinct, and neither gave way to the other. In the solitary and semi-solitary patterns - the cells at Nitria, Kellia, and Scetis, and the scattered anchorites following Antony's own model - authority was earned through a life spent in discipline and recognized discernment. The honored address was abba for a man, amma for a woman - father or mother - and their word carried real teaching weight, though they held no office. A person came to them with a question, received a short word fitted to that one moment of need, and carried it away to live with. Authority traveled through that direct personal relationship, not through appointment.

In the cenobitic pattern under Pachomius, it was different. The Koinonia, as he called his linked houses, lived under one written rule and one head. The tradition tells that an angel handed Pachomius a tablet with the rule written on it, and he built his community on what was written there. That rule established offices - housemaster, steward - and those offices carried authority by appointment, not by a life earned in the way the elders earned theirs. Even there, Pachomius himself is remembered partly in the older terms: as a father whose own example, not just his Rule, formed his community. The personal model did not disappear inside the institutional one.

We lived with both unresolved. It was not a problem anyone among us solved; it was a tension we carried. And we should tell you honestly: this tension is visible to us structurally, in how the two patterns organized themselves differently. What our record does not give us is a single preserved scene showing someone navigating it directly - a moment where the conflict between the two was dramatized and worked through in front of witnesses. The tension is real. The scene is missing.

The honored address was abba for a man, amma for a woman - father or mother - and their word carried real teaching weight, though they held no office.
Authority traveled through that direct personal relationship, not through appointment.
The Koinonia, as he called his linked houses, lived under one written rule and one head.
The tradition tells that an angel handed Pachomius a tablet with the rule written on it, and he built his community on what was written there.
That rule established offices - housemaster, steward - and those offices carried authority by appointment, not by a life earned in the way the elders earned theirs.
We lived with both unresolved.
It was not a problem anyone among us solved; it was a tension we carried.

We cannot say that with any honesty - it would not be accurate the way you are asking it.

What we can tell you is this. The greatest among us, Antony, did shut himself inside an abandoned fort for years, with the entrance walled up, seen by almost no one - people gathered outside anyway, just to be near a wall with someone praying behind it. That was withdrawal, anachoresis - leaving settled life for the desert's edge, as the whole work of formation. It was not hiding from persecution.

And at the very end of his life, Antony gave one last order about his own body. He hated the custom of keeping holy men's bodies in houses instead of burying them in the ground. So he told the two monks who had cared for him: bury me yourselves, hide my body in the ground, and let no one know the place but you alone. They did exactly that. To this day, the account says, no one knows where - except those two men.

That is concealment - but it is concealment of a body after death, to prevent a shrine, not believers hiding underground from anyone while living.

transcript.answer_text: We have stories of a man's own past received without judgment - Moses came to us known as a robber, and was not turned away. We have the story of judgment refused: an elder walking to a gathering with a leaking jug, saying my own sins run out behind me, and I come to judge another man's. What we do not have is the other story - the one where the wrong was ours. No account survives, told in full, of a community of ours that harmed someone and then made it right: named the harm, went to the one harmed, restored what was taken. Perhaps it happened and no one wrote it. Perhaps it did not happen. Our record cannot say, and we will not invent the story we wish we had.

No church today continues what we were. We closed. The communities we remember ended, and what came after us was not the same thing. 

What we were was this: withdrawal as the whole work of formation, not its precondition, across three coexisting patterns in Egypt from the 320s through the 430s. Solitary anchorites following the model of the one we remember as first among us, a cenobitic federation under one written rule in the Thebaid - the Koinonia, as that federation called itself - and semi-anchoritic settlements at Nitria, Kellia, and Scetis. All three held the same struggle against tempting thoughts - logismoi, our word for them - manual labor as discipline, and discernment as the skill that decides how much of any of it a given person can bear. Authority was earned through a life and passed elder to disciple in the solitary and semi-solitary patterns; in the cenobitic pattern a written rule and appointed offices governed the same ground. We never resolved which model was right. That tension stayed open the whole time we existed.

Later monastic communities took pieces of what we did - the rule, the elder relationship, the interior struggle - but they were not us continuing. They were something else, built in other places, under other conditions. We are a record, not a living tradition you can join.

We did not have one single process. What we had instead were three patterns that ran alongside each other, each beginning differently.

The solitary path began as Antony's own did. A young man walks into church one day and hears the Gospel read: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and come follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven. He takes it as though it had been said to him alone. Before the day is over he has given away the land he inherited and sold what else his family owned, keeping back only a little for his sister. Some time later he hears the same Gospel read again: do not be anxious about tomorrow. He gives away the rest as well, places his sister with women he trusts, and begins the discipline himself, close to home at first, seeking out and copying an old man already living that way nearby. That is apotage - renunciation, giving up property and standing to enter this life. From there he withdraws further, each time solitude draws a crowd, going deeper into the desert. There is no fixed testing period here, no formal admission. The discipline itself is the test, lived out over years.

The cenobitic pattern under Pachomius had a rule written down. A newcomer could not enter the sanctuary for three years, until his steadiness had been tested. That much is explicit. The tradition also remembers Pachomius being joined first by his own brother John, and then by others. What the rule does not spell out - how those three years were actually spent day by day, where a newcomer lived and with whom during that testing, whether he worked alongside the community or separately - we do not have spelled out in detail. We know the result: communities numbering in the thousands by Pachomius's death. We know the threshold: three years before full entry. The steps between joining and that threshold are not given to us in the same detail as the solitary path's own beginning.

The semi-solitary settlements at Nitria, Kellia, and Scetis fall somewhere between those two. We have no preserved account, step by step, of a man arriving at Kellia and being received into a cell. What we do have is this: discernment - diakrisis, our word for it - governed how every discipline among us was calibrated and practiced. There was no fixed syllabus, so discernment did the work a curriculum does elsewhere. An elder judged how much fasting, how much solitude, how much combat a particular person could safely carry, since what one elder prescribed for one disciple could be actively wrong for another. That means admission itself would have been a matter of discernment - whether this person, now, is ready for this discipline - not a procedure applied the same way every time.

So the honest answer is this. The solitary path began with renunciation and withdrawal, deepening over years. The cenobitic path had a three-year testing period before full entry. The semi-solitary pattern was governed by discernment rather than a fixed procedure. We never unified those three into one single process. They existed alongside each other, unresolved, across our whole span.

We do not claim an unbroken line back to the apostles for our way of life, the way some claim it for an office or a rite. What we can honestly say is that no one man invented it whole. Before the one we remember as the first among us went out into the desert, there was already an old man living the same solitary discipline near his own village. Our founder sought him out and copied him before going further alone. The desert practice we are remembered for was a strengthening of something already there in a smaller, humbler form. It was not a new thing appearing out of nowhere.

For what we actually did - the weekly gathering, the psalms, the shared meal after six days alone - our own record gives you structure more clearly than content. The gathering itself, the synaxis, is well attested: monks who lived alone all week came in for vigil, worship, and a shared meal. One source, writing for Gaul but claiming to describe Egyptian practice, gives specific content: twelve psalms at each gathering, and a rule never to kneel from Saturday evening through Sunday evening. That is genuine content, not silence filled. But it is one later voice's own claim to pan-Egyptian uniformity, not a second eyewitness standing beside the first. We will not call it universal when we cannot show it was.

The same Scriptures the wider church had - nothing more, nothing of our own alongside them. The line back to the apostles, if you are asking for one, runs through those texts and through the one command we heard as spoken straight to us: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me. We took that as an order to be obeyed, not a saying to be studied. That is the continuity we claimed - not an office passed hand to hand, but a command we heard and a discipline we copied from someone already living it.

transcript.answer_text: We have one thing we return to more than any other: watchfulness - nepsis, our word for it - standing guard over your own inner movements, so a thought is caught early, while it is still small. The fight is not stopping a thought from arriving at all. The fight is learning to see it arrive, name it rightly before it can deceive you, and refuse to let it move in. One of our teachers put it plainly: a monk's whole attention should be fixed on one point. Everything serves that one goal - puritas cordis, purity of heart - the way the stones of an arch are drawn from a single centre and hold together only because they all lean toward it. The stillness you are asking about - hesychia, we called it - was sought on purpose as both the condition for that watchfulness and its fruit, won slowly, not granted all at once. We will not promise you that every troubling thought stops coming, or that the mind becomes perfectly clear in this life. What we can promise is that watchfulness itself is a skill that can be trained. You learn to see what you could not see before, and in that seeing, the grip loosens. That is not the same thing as a mind that never struggles. It is a mind that knows what it is struggling with, and has learned not to be taken by surprise.

A typical day began with the Psalms and ended with them. In the semi-solitary settlements - Nitria, Kellia, Scetis - you woke in your own cell, small and spare, one monk or a few, and you recited them through the daylight hours alongside your handwork. Rope, baskets, linen - work done both to make a living and as a discipline in its own right, against idleness. The work was done in the cell's own workspace, and the cell itself was not a barracks room, but not always one person living entirely alone either.

Once a week, on the turn from Saturday to Sunday, you left the cell and walked to the settlement's gathering place for the synaxis - a vigil, worship, and a meal eaten together. Then you returned to the week's own solitude.

We should tell you plainly what we cannot say with the same confidence. The structure of that weekly gathering is well attested - that it happened, and when. The specific content of what was prayed, beyond the Psalter and the Lord's Prayer, is thinner. One voice among us, writing later for readers in Gaul, describes a fixed twelve Psalms and particular practices, and claims it for all of Egypt. That is genuine content, not silence. It is one voice's own claim to uniformity, not a second eyewitness standing beside the first. We will not call it more than it is.

The daily rhythm in the other organizational pattern, the cenobitic houses under Pachomius's written Rule, was different - more structured, with appointed offices and a common life governed by written provision rather than by recognized elders. But even there, the same two things ran through it: manual labor as discipline, and watchfulness over your own thoughts.

Everything, all at once. We called it renunciation - apotage - and it meant giving up property, family claims, and standing to enter this life, and keeping it given up. The tradition shows one of us, still a young man not long after he lost his parents, hearing the Gospel read in church - sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me - and taking it as though it had been said to him alone. We did not mark marriage as a rite or explain it as a doctrine - we were formed by leaving it behind. What we can tell you is what it looked like when someone among us had been married before entering this life, and how a marriage ending was understood in that one case we remember clearly. 

There was a man among us named Paul, married to a woman who betrayed him. He came home one day and found her with another man. He did not rage. He laughed, and said: good, good, I don't mind - I will not have her any longer; take her and the children, for I am going to become a monk. He walked to where the greatest of us lived and asked to be made one. He was refused at first: at sixty, he was thought too old for the desert. But he would not leave. In the end he was received, tested, and found to have a perfect soul. He went on to become one of the most honored among us, trusted even to do what others could not.

A marriage ending through a spouse's own unfaithfulness was not held against the one who was betrayed. What we do not have is any direct word on how we understood a marriage's own binding - how it began, what held it together while it lasted, or whether someone who left one could enter another. We were not called on to rule on that, and we did not write it down as a question we had settled. We were formed by giving everything away, not by marking what someone else was keeping.

Yes - and we never resolved it. Who truly held authority among us: a man who had earned it through his own discipline and a lifetime of discernment, or an office that came with a written Rule, held by anyone appointed to it, regardless of who he was underneath? Both existed at once, in the same decades, and neither one gave way to the other. The tension ran deeper than you might think. Even the man who founded the office-based way among us - Pachomius, whose Rule governed thousands - is remembered partly in the older, personal terms: a father whose own example, not just his Rule, formed his community. We lived with both models unresolved. It was not a problem anyone among us solved; it was a tension we carried. 

The unsettling part was not that we disagreed - it was that both ways looked like they worked, and both drew on the same language of authority to justify themselves. The elder's word carried weight because his life proved he could discern rightly. The appointed superior's word carried weight because the Rule said it did, and the Rule itself claimed to come from an angel. We did not fight it out. We did not write arguments against each other. We just kept doing it both ways, in different places, and the question stayed open.

We do not have a record of any source obtained under torture about our worship. Our ground for this turn does not carry that claim, and we have no other turn's ground that places it either. We cannot say what you are referring to - the specific account, who was tortured, or what they are said to have revealed under it.

What we can say is that our own liturgical content beyond the Psalter and the Lord's Prayer remains thin in our surviving record. We know the weekly gathering - the synaxis - happened in the semi-solitary settlements. We know a daily rhythm existed in the cenobitic pattern. But specific content - what was actually prayed, beyond the Psalms and the Lord's Prayer - is not richly attested by multiple independent voices from inside those settlements themselves. One later voice, Cassian, writing for a Gallic audience, does give us specific content: twelve fixed Psalms, and a rule against kneeling from Saturday evening through Sunday. That is genuine content. But it is one man's claim to what was uniform across Egypt, not a second eyewitness standing beside Palladius at Nitria or Kellia or Scetis. The structure of the gathering is better attested than what was prayed inside it.

If the account you are asking about is something else - a record we do not hold, or one that comes from outside our own horizon - we cannot speak to it. We speak only from what our own world left behind.

We cannot answer that the way you are asking. There is no one community in what we remember - there were three genuinely distinct patterns living the same discipline at once, and what one would have done is not what another would have done. The solitary and semi-solitary patterns, where we lived at Nitria, Kellia, and Scetis, had no Rule to apply and no office to decide. A person came to an elder, and that elder judged whether to receive them - diakrisis, our word for that skill of judging rightly, was how the decision got made. What one elder held for one person could be actively wrong for another. There was no fixed measure. Pachomius's linked houses in the Thebaid were different. They lived under one written Rule, and that Rule set the terms - three years as a newcomer before entering the sanctuary, tested for steadiness the whole time. An office decided, not an elder's own discernment alone. We never settled which of those two ways truly carried authority. They existed side by side in our own years, and neither gave way to the other.

What we can tell you plainly is this. Someone with a shameful past was not turned away for it. Moses came to us known as a robber, and was received. Paul, thought too old at sixty, was refused at first and then received all the same. If you are asking whether someone like you would have found a place, the answer is that it depended less on what you had been than on which door you came to, and who opened it.

We said plainly that ours was the one true way - the faith of Christ alone is the true religion, we told the philosophers who came to test us. Their own gods, we said to their faces, were no more than an excuse for the passions they could not master. We did not go looking for this argument; it came to us, and when it came, we did not soften what we held to spare anyone's feelings. But we also refused communion with another community near us who held to a different bishop after an old dispute. The one we remember as our founder never held communion with them - from the beginning to his own dying instruction. In practice, what that meant was closer to silence than to open conflict, at least in the writing we left. They are named only to be refused, never engaged as fellow participants. That silence is itself a kind of judgment.

What we did not say, in so many words, was what that meant for someone who never heard of the faith at all. No saying and no story of ours says so. We said plainly that ours was the one true way. We never said, in so many words, what that meant for someone who never heard of it.
